newsitem.title: USA: Calif. lumber firm may resume salvage logging.
newsitem.headline: Calif. lumber firm may resume salvage logging.

text.p: California officials gave a lumber company permission to resume the controversial logging of fallen trees in an ancient redwood forest Thursday but set strict conditions.

The California Department of Forestry ordered Pacific Lumber Co to temporarily halt salvage logging in All Species grove -- an old-growth redwood grove in northern California -- Wednesday because lumber workers cut down a standing tree, violating a permit that allowed the company to log only dead, dying or diseased trees.
The department said it rescinded the order Thursday after meeting with Pacific Lumber officials at their headquarters in Scotia, California.
Robert Irelan, spokesman for MAXXAM Inc, Pacific Lumber's parent company, said Pacific Lumber expected to resume salvage operations Friday.

California, the U.S. government and MAXXAM reached a tentative agreement last month to set aside two ancient redwood groves for parks, in return for $380 million in cash and land and a promise to smooth environmental problems. A moratorium on salvage logging is in place in those two groves.

But Pacific Lumber has a permit to cut 10 percent of dead, dying or diseased timber in four other old-growth groves and it began the salvage logging Monday, angering environmentalists who are fighting to preserve all of the groves.

The California Department of Forestry set several restrictions on the salvage logging, saying crews must not cut down any standing tree and must reduce the risk of damage to standing trees by using two tractors to drag out fallen logs and cutting logs into shorter lengths.
It said Pacific Lumber must consult with the department if damage to standing trees was likely and if damage was unavoidable, they could not salvage the fallen tree.
The California Department of Forestry and the Department of Fish and Game said they would make daily inspections of salvage operations.
